title: Request parsing & event-loop CPU audit (epoll + JSON path)
content:
Summary:

Short version: we found that a sizable portion of short text-generation requests (<= 128 tokens) spend ~30–45% of CPU time in request parsing and framework dispatch on our Python + uvicorn stack even when the model runtime is offloaded to GPUs. The dominant subcomponents are JSON decoding, header auth checks (regex-heavy), and the async-to-thread switching overhead when calling the tokenizer preproc.

Why we looked: teams reported p95 latency regressions under moderate qps (200–500 rps) even though GPU tokenization and inference looked fine. Hypothesis was CPU-side ingress work (parsing, validation, routing) saturates worker-side cores.

Key findings (high-level):
- JSON parsing (stdlib json.loads in our request handler) accounted for ~18–30% of per-request CPU at p95 in microbenchmarks. Replacing with orjson reduced that to ~3–8%.
- Python-level header validation using multiple compiled regexes for tenant tokens was ~5–12% of CPU; moving to a single compiled parse reduced it by ~60%.
- Async/Sync boundary (loop.run_in_executor + thread pool handoff for tokenizer) introduced 2–6ms extra tail latency for small requests due to context switching and queue contention when threadpool size is mis-tuned.
- epoll/wake-up overhead visible in eBPF traces when we had many short-lived connections (keepalive disabled) — frequent accept/close dominates syscalls.

Methodology + artifacts:
- Workloads: replayed production traffic traces (sanitized) and synthetic short-request benchmark: 50% chat-turn, 30% expand, 20% embeddings; typical payload 200–800 bytes.
- Load tools: wrk2 (fixed-rate), vegeta for attack patterns, and a custom async client that keeps TCP keepalive on.
- Profilers: py-spy (sampling), perf + FlameGraph, eBPF (bcc) scripts for syscalls, and strace on a subset.
- Commands (examples):
  - wrk2 -t8 -c200 -R400 -d120s --latency http://localhost:8000/generate
  - PYTHONPATH=. /usr/bin/python -m py-spy record -o profile.svg --pid <worker-pid>
  - sudo perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 60; perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded; flamegraph.pl out.folded > perf.svg

Microbenchmarks (single-worker local):
- Baseline (uvicorn + stdlib json + run_in_executor tokenizer): p50=6.2ms p95=18.7ms CPU util per core 78% @ 400 rps
- Replace json.loads -> orjson.loads: p50=5.1ms p95=11.4ms CPU util per core 55% @ 400 rps
- Precompile header parse, reduce regexes: p95 improves further to ~9.2ms
- Move small tokenizer into async Python (avoid threadpool): lowered tail only when tokenizer implementation is pure Python and async-friendly; when native libs involved threadpool still wins.

Flamegraph/eBPF observations (notes from traces):
- Flamegraph top stacks were dominated by: PyObject_Call, _PyEval_EvalFrameDefault, _json.c:decode_obj, re.py:findall and asyncio.base_tasks.Task.__step__ (loop->thread handoff).
- perf showed syscall hotspots: epoll_wait, accept, close when keepalive disabled; with keepalive enabled, syscall cost reduced ~40% and CPU shifted to Python parsing code.
- eBPF syscall histogram showed spikes in futex and epoll_ctl at burst edges (indicates threadpool contention).

Root causes we believe are actionable: 
1) Use of slow JSON decoder and heavy Python-side validation per request.
2) Frequent short-lived connections causing syscall churn (accept/close/epoll).
3) Suboptimal async/thread pool configuration for tokenizer bridging.
4) Extra copies between Python bytes and tokenizer native bindings for small payloads.

Experiments tried and results: 
- Fast JSON: orjson gave the largest single-win. Note: we had to adjust error handling because orjson raises different exceptions. Side benefit: reduced memory churn.
- Keep-Alive tuning: enabling keepalive and raising connection limits reduced syscall CPU by ~35% at 400 rps. For long-lived clients this is recommended.
- Pre-parse header: moved auth token prefix detection to C-accelerated prefix check (using startswith on bytes) before regex; reduced CPU for auth path by ~60%.
- Tokenizer options: evaluated three options:
  * Keep Python tokenizer in run_in_executor (current): predictable but threadpool contention at high concurrency.
  * Move to async-friendly Rust tokenizer via pyo3 (single-threaded awaitable): reduced context switches, lowered p95 by ~10% in small-request regime.
  * Shared tokenizer service (local gRPC): eliminated per-worker threadpool but added IPC overhead; helpful where tokenizer is heavy and can be cached.
- Threadpool tuning: increasing max_workers from default 8->24 helped at 800 rps but increased tail when host CPU saturated. Dynamic autosizing based on backlog improved stability.

Recommendations (short/mid/long term):
- Short term (low risk):
  * Replace stdlib json with orjson in request path (patch in PR 718).
  * Enable TCP keepalive by default for hosted edge and recommend client SDK to reuse connections.
  * Precompile header parsing and remove repeated regex calls; adopt simple byte-prefix checks where possible.
- Mid term (moderate effort):
  * Expose tokenizer isolation knob: allow customers to choose threadpool vs async-Rust tokenizer in config. Add telemetry for threadpool queue wait time.
  * Add a lightweight ingress filter (C-extension or Rust) that does minimal JSON schema validation and header checks before handing off to Python. This can be gated behind a feature flag.
- Long term (architectural):
  * Consider moving the HTTP ingress layer from Python workers to a thin proxy in Rust (actix/tide) that performs parsing/auth and forwards a compact binary payload to Python/gRPC or model runtime. Benefits: fewer copies, less Python overhead per-request, better syscall/multiplexing.

Operational guidance:
- Monitor metrics to add: request_parse_time p50/p95, threadpool_queue_time, tcp_keepalive_reused_connections_percent, json_decode_errors, tokenizer_wait_time.
- Alerting: trigger if request_parse_time p95 increases >20% vs baseline for 5m or if threadpool_queue_time > 10ms for >1% of requests.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Is full ingress offload to Rust net/proxy worth the deployment complexity for Dedicated customers? Do a cost/ops analysis.
- Measure the impact of switching SSL termination to the host proxy vs within uvicorn (we suspect per-request SSL handshakes are rare, but TLS record patterns may affect epoll behavior).
- Evaluate using UNIX domain sockets between proxy and Python worker to remove TCP overhead for local routing.

Appendix (notes/snippets):
- Quick orjson integration pattern:
  try:
    body = orjson.loads(req.body)
  except orjson.JSONDecodeError as e:
    return JSONResponse(status_code=400, content={"error":"invalid json"})

- Example eBPF one-liner used to see accept/close rates:
  sudo /usr/share/bcc/tools/syscount -f -c 1s | grep -E "accept|close|epoll_wait"

- Perf tip: sample frequency 99hz gave stable flamegraphs for p95 analysis; py-spy useful to get Python symbol resolution without instrumenting.

Owners / follow-ups:
- Aisha to land orjson patch and telemetry hooks (PR 718).
- Kenji to prototype Rust async tokenizer binding and run quants.
- Lina to run a dedicated customer simulation with keepalive toggled and document results.

If you want a trimmed checklist for a quick roll:
- [ ] Cherry-pick orjson change to canary
- [ ] Enable keepalive for canary clients and measure syscall delta
- [ ] Add threadpool_queue_time metric
- [ ] Prototype ingress filter in Rust (POC)

Notes to self: this doc is intentionally a grab-bag of traces and decisions; will move final recommendations into a Confluence design doc if we decide to pursue a proxy rewrite.
